newsitem.title: USA: Kemp card beats OJ, Namath; 'Bathtub Ladies' rise.
newsitem.headline: Kemp card beats OJ, Namath; 'Bathtub Ladies' rise.

text.p: Jack Kemp, the former pro football quarterback now running for vice president, is No. 1 on at least one score: his 1965 football card is trading more often than "Broadway" Joe Namath's and leaves O.J. Simpson's card in the dust.

Kemp, Bob Dole's Republican running-mate, has the fastest-moving football card traded these days, from when he played for the Buffalo Bills. Valued at $200, the Kemp card has gained 20 percent since he entered the White House race, according to Greg Ambrosius, editor of Sports Cards magazine.

Ambrosius said Kemp displaced formerly best-selling Namath, a star quarterback for the New York Jets, whose 1965 rookie card is still the most valuable football card at $1,650, but isn't turning over as fast as Kemp's.

Astute collectors are likely to hold on to their Kemp cards, Ambrosius said: "If he became vice president right now, there's no question his card numbers would continue to go up." And a presidential bid in the year 2000 would add even more value to the Kemp card.

By contrast, Simpson's cards from when he played for the Bills are "pretty much dead in the water," Ambrosius said by telephone from Iola, Wisconsin. Simpson, whose civil trial in the deaths of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman is proceeding, had a 1970 card priced at $100, but sellers "had trouble moving it even at $75," the editor said.
On the campaign trail, Kemp's political "quarterback," Dole, has been savoring the delights of Middle America. Plain coffee, for instance.

The former Kansas senator takes his coffee plain, as reporters learned when Dole visited a family in Willoughby, Ohio. It turns out that "plain" means "black" in this case, which suits the plain-spoken, no-frills Dole to a T.
Back in Washington, there is a tardy and possibly temporary victory for women's rights. "The Ladies in the Bathtub" is moving upstairs, but perhaps only for a year.

The "Ladies" are Susan B. Anthony, Lucretia Mott and Elizabeth Cady Stanton, immortalised in marble. A statue commemorating them, which was dedicated in 1921, languished in storage at the U.S. Capitol until being moved to a first-floor exhibit area known as The Crypt a few years ago.

A resolution sponsored by Representative Connie Morella, a Maryland Republican who is up for re-election this year, passed by both the House and Senate provides for the massive work to be moved up to the Capitol Rotunda, where the statues of famous men are shown.

The move, which will cost an estimated $75,000, could be temporary. The "Ladies" -- so nicknamed because the statue shows busts of the three feminists emerging from a solid block of marble -- will stay in the Rotunda for a year while a commission decides where its permanent place should be.
The statue's official title is "Portrait Monument."
Elsewhere on Capitol Hill, "awesome abs" and just a hint of chest hair were on display after nine male congressional staffers earned a "dreamy" rating from the teen magazine Sassy.
The nine were photographed for the magazine following a slight makeover which in some cases included changing shoes, bleaching hair and baring stomachs.

Christopher Chapel, a senior legislative aide to Florida Republican Representative Cliff Stearns, was shown on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial with his shirt unbuttoned to reveal what Sassy called "awesome abs".
Chapel told The Hill magazine that he participated as a lark and to help convey the message that "It's OK to succeed, it's OK to be involved in politics ... and you can still be cool."
